sentences.sentence: Episode length is the failure detector that zero-shot reward models must beat, and how hard it is to beat depends on who stopped the episode.
On a public SO-101 benchmark that anyone can rerun, where runs end at a time limit, length alone separates failure from success at AUROC 0.942 within policy.
It does not need the timeout.
Watched only up to half of the longest episode, it still gives 0.851, because failed runs are slow rather than cut off.
Both reward models we test, run zero-shot, score below it, the better one at 0.821.

Our own rollouts, which an operator stopped by judgment, reverse the picture: length falls to 0.56, and what catches failures is a judge that sees the finished episode, passing its threshold at an operating point chosen in-sample.
No mid-episode monitor reaches its bar.
So report a within-policy length baseline, and name the dataset's stopping rule.
A reward model that scores robot rollouts is also a failure detector, and papers evaluate it as one, mostly against other learned detectors.
The baseline that matters is often simpler.
When a benchmark stops failed runs at a time limit, the length of an episode encodes its outcome, and so does the identity of the policy that ran (we call the second one the policy-identity null).
When an operator stops each run by judgment, both signals collapse and the detection task changes with them.
Which of the two a dataset uses is its *stopping rule*, and none of the reward-model papers in our library reports it or the length baseline it implies.
We started with a narrower claim, that elapsed time is the reward model to beat.
Our own rollouts broke it.
On them length is near chance while a robot-trained judge passed its pre-registered threshold, and since the stopping rule is what separates the two results, it became the subject of the paper.

We measured length on a public SO-101 benchmark and on our own rollouts, with the length analyses frozen before any number existed, and set against it two zero-shot reward models and every judge and monitor we had run on our 88 operator-stopped rollouts.
ArmnetBench v0.1 covers the SO-101 with 8 tasks and 7 policies.
We use its 2,047 policy rollouts with a success or failure class (515 successes, 1,532 failures) and leave out the teleoperated episodes.
One task, pushing a Displayport cable (270 rollouts), has rollouts of a single class and so no per-task AUROC.
Our own data are 88 labelled bowls-task episodes on one SO-101 arm with a Jetson Orin NX, and the 50-episode subset (42 successes, 8 failures) that every monitor gate used.
The author was the operator: he stopped each run and labelled it at rest, not blind to the policy.
On ArmnetBench, episode length is a strong failure detector, and not only because it tells the policies apart (Table 1, Fig. 1).
Pooled over policies it reaches 0.938.
Within each policy it ranges from 0.91 to 0.96, or 0.942 pair-weighted, with a CI of 0.927–0.956.
Both reward models, run zero-shot, fall below it on this benchmark.
Robometer-4B, as its authors ship it, scores 0.818 pooled and 0.821 within policy (pair-weighted over its per-policy scores, whose range stands in for a CI; §7 says why).
TOPReward, with Qwen3-VL-8B and no training, scores 0.661 within policy, and its paired difference to length has a 95 % CI of -0.31 to -0.25.
The protocols fixed each model's primary score before any score existed (Robometer's success probability, and the success score of TOPReward's paper).
The two descriptive rows of Table 1, read from the same runs, score higher but still below length.

sentences.section: 5 Judges and monitors on our rollouts

sentences.sentence: The second version catches 3 of 8 at 5 of 42, with AUROC 0.79 against 0.71 when its actions are shuffled, and its MLP variant catches 6 of 8 but flags 13 of 42.
Robometer and TOPReward are the two reward models we test.

Robometer scales a general-purpose reward model through trajectory comparisons, TOPReward reads the token probabilities of a video-language model as hidden rewards, while a survey of verifiers for robot policies maps the wider family.
Our monitors borrow from the mid-episode line of work.
FAIL-Detect and SAFE learn uncertainty- and feature-based failure scores for imitation and VLA policies.
FARM reads failure signals from the internal states of a frozen world model, close to our world-model monitors, and ReAP predicts action-conditioned risk, the idea behind our risk head.
VLA-Corrector, Spotter and REMORA add stage verification, a reflecting VLM and recurrent progress tracking.
ArmnetBench and a standardized SO-101 VLA benchmark evaluate policies on the same low-cost arm.
None of these works reports the elapsed-length baseline under the dataset's stopping rule, and that comparison is what this paper adds.
The judge pass on our own rollouts rests on 8 failures and on operating thresholds chosen on the same 50 episodes, labelled by a single operator, the author, who was not blind to the policy.
The threshold-free AUROCs do not depend on that choice, and fresh rollouts scored at the frozen thresholds are the confirming test.
Policy identity is a second confound: 17 of the 25 failures in our 69 rollouts are TurboVLA's, so any score that reads the policy gets the policy-identity null for free.
The risk head is trained and tested on the same 50 episodes (five folds by episode keep episodes from leaking, but tasks and policies do leak).

Robometer's within-policy number has no episode-bootstrap CI and Robometer is missing from the truncation analysis, because its per-episode scores stayed on an older machine; a copy from that machine or a re-score of about $6 would restore both.
TOPReward's paper does not give its prefix count, frames per query or Yes/No wording, so those are our choices.
The ArmnetBench result covers eight tasks, and the timeout is approximated by each task's longest episode.
Before evaluating a reward model as a failure detector, run episode length within policy on the same rows, and say how the episodes ended.
On a benchmark that stops at a time limit, length was the detector to beat, and neither reward model beat it.
On rollouts an operator stopped, length was useless, and what caught failures was a judge that saw the whole finished episode in the right input format.
